entries.2f87740dc2df76ead79f3d2e049a71379f73fdf0: <div sID="gen11813" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="74" osisID="Ps.74" sID="Ps.74"/> <div eID="gen11813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11814" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11815" type="x-p"/> This psalm does so particularly describe the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, by Nebuchadnezzar and the army of the Chaldeans, and can so ill be applied to any other event we meet with in the Jewish history, that interpreters incline to think that either it was penned by David, or Asaph in David's time, with a prophetical reference to that sad event (which yet is not so probable), or that it was penned by another Asaph, who lived at the time of the captivity, or by Jeremiah (for it is of a piece with his Lamentations,) or some other prophet, and, after the return out of captivity, was delivered to the sons of Asaph, who were called by his name, for the public service of the church. That was the most eminent family of the singers in Ezra's time. See <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.41 Ezra.3.10 Neh.11.17 Neh.11.22">Ezra ii. 41; iii. 10; Neh. xi. 17, 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.35 Neh.12.46">xii. 35, 46</reference>. The deplorable case of the people of God at that time is here spread before the Lord, and left with him. The prophet, in the name of the church I. Puts in complaining pleas of the miseries they suffered, for the quickening of their desires in prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.1-Ps.74.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. He puts in comfortable pleas for the encouraging of their faith in prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.12-Ps.74.17">ver. 12-17</reference>. III. He concludes with divers petitions to God for deliverances, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.18-Ps.74.23">ver. 18-23</reference>. In singing it we must be affected with the former desolations of the church, for we are members of the same body, and may apply it to any present distresses or desolations of any part of the Christian church.
entries.145aa8dc5ee4cb19c5db3f781f314b4ceb4b3d4e: <div eID="gen11815" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11814" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Mournful Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen11816" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O God, why hast thou cast <hi type="italic">us</hi> off for ever? <hi type="italic">why</hi> doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture? <hi type="super">2</hi> Remember thy congregation, <hi type="italic">which</hi> thou hast purchased of old; the rod of thine inheritance, <hi type="italic">which</hi> thou hast redeemed; this mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt. <hi type="super">3</hi> Lift up thy feet unto the perpetual desolations; <hi type="italic">even</hi> all <hi type="italic">that</hi> the enemy hath done wickedly in the sanctuary. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thine enemies roar in the midst of thy congregations; they set up their ensigns <hi type="italic">for</hi> signs. <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">A man</hi> was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees. <hi type="super">6</hi> But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers. <hi type="super">7</hi> They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled <hi type="italic">by casting down</hi> the dwelling place of thy name to the ground. <hi type="super">8</hi> They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land. <hi type="super">9</hi> We see not our signs: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no more any prophet: neither <hi type="italic">is there</hi> among us any that knoweth how long. <hi type="super">10</hi> O God, how long shall the adversary reproach? shall the enemy blaspheme thy name for ever? <hi type="super">11</hi> Why withdrawest thou thy hand, even thy right hand? pluck <hi type="italic">it</hi> out of thy bosom. <div eID="gen11816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11817" type="x-p"/> This psalm is entitled <hi type="italic">Maschil—a psalm to give instruction,</hi> for it was penned in a day of affliction, which is intended for instruction; and this instruction in general it gives us, That when we are, upon any account, in distress, it is our wisdom and duty to apply to God by faithful and fervent prayer, and we shall not find it in vain to do so. Three things the people of God here complain of:— <div eID="gen11817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11818" type="x-p"/> I. The displeasure of God against them, as that which was the cause and bitterness of all their calamities. They look above the instruments of their trouble, who, they knew, could have no power against them unless it were given them from above, and keep their eye upon God, by whose determined counsel they were delivered up into the hands of wicked and unreasonable men. Observe the liberty they take to expostulate with God (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">v. 1</reference>), we hope not too great a liberty, for Christ himself, upon the cross, cried out, <hi type="italic">My God my God, why hast thou forsaken me?</hi> So the church here, <hi type="italic">O God! why hast thou forsaken us for ever?</hi> Here they speak according to their present dark and melancholy apprehensions; for otherwise, <hi type="italic">Has God cast away his people? God forbid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>. The people of God must not think that because they are cast down they are therefore cast off, that because men cast them off therefore God does, and that because he seems to cast them off for a time therefore they are really cast off for ever: yet this expostulation intimates that they dreaded God's casting them off more than any thing, that they desired to be owned of him, whatever they suffered from men, and were desirous to know wherefore he thus contended with them: <hi type="italic">Why does thy anger smoke?</hi> that is, why does it rise up to such a degree that all about us take notice of it, and ask, <hi type="italic">What means the heat of this great anger?</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.24">Deut. xxix. 24</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.29.20">v. 20</reference>, where the anger of the Lord and his jealousy are said to smoke against sinners. Observe what they plead with God, now that they lay under the tokens and apprehensions of his wrath. 1. They plead their relation to him: "We are <hi type="italic">the sheep of thy pasture,</hi> the sheep wherewith thou hast been pleased to stock the pasture, thy peculiar people whom thou art pleased to set apart for thyself and design for thy own glory. That the wolves worry the sheep is not strange; but was ever any shepherd thus displeased at his own sheep? <hi type="italic">Remember,</hi> we are <hi type="italic">thy congregation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.2">v. 2</reference>), incorporated by thee and for thee, and devoted to thy praise; we are <hi type="italic">the rod,</hi> or tribe, <hi type="italic">of thy inheritance,</hi> whom thou hast been pleased to claim a special property in above other people ( <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">Deut. xxxii. 9</reference>), and from whom thou hast received the rents and issues of praise and worship more than from the neighbouring nations. Nay, a man's inheritance may lie at a great distance, but we are pleading for <hi type="italic">Mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt,</hi> which has been the place of thy peculiar delight and residence, thy demesne and mansion." 2. They plead the great things God had done for them and the vast expense he had been at upon them: "It is <hi type="italic">thy congregation,</hi> which thou hast not only made with a word's speaking, but <hi type="italic">purchased of old</hi> by many miracles of mercy when they were first formed into a people; it is <hi type="italic">thy inheritance, which thou hast redeemed</hi> when they were sold into servitude." God <hi type="italic">gave Egypt</hi> to ruin <hi type="italic">for their ransom, gave men for them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">people for their life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3-Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 3, 4</reference>. "Now, Lord, wilt thou now abandon a people that cost thee so dear, and has been so dear to thee?" And, if the redemption of Israel out of Egypt was an encouragement to hope that he would not cast them off, much more reason have we to hope that God will not cast off any whom Christ has redeemed with his own blood; but the people of his purchase shall be for ever the people of his praise. 3. They plead the calamitous state that they were in (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lift up thy feet;</hi> that is, come with speed to repair the desolations that are made in thy sanctuary, which otherwise will be perpetual an irreparable." It has been sometimes said that the divine vengeance strikes with iron hands, yet it comes with leaden feet; and then those who wait for the day of the Lord, cry, <hi type="italic">Lord, lift up thy feet; exalt thy steps;</hi> magnify thyself in the outgoing of thy providence. When the desolations of the sanctuary have continued long we are tempted to think they will be perpetual; but it is a temptation; for God will avenge his own elect, will avenge them speedily, though he bear long with their oppressors and persecutors. <div eID="gen11818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11819" type="x-p"/> II. They complain of the outrage and cruelty of their enemies, not so much, no, not at all, of what they had done to the prejudice of their secular interests; here are no complaints of the burning of their cities and ravaging of their country, but only what they had done against the sanctuary and the synagogue. The concerns of religion should lie nearer our hearts and affect us more than any worldly concern whatsoever. The desolation of God's house should grieve us more than the desolation of our own houses; for the matter is not great what becomes of us and our families in this world provided God's name may be sanctified, his kingdom may come, and his will be done. <div eID="gen11819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11820" type="x-p"/> 1. The psalmist complains of the desolations of the sanctuary, as Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.17">ch. ix. 17</reference>. The temple at Jerusalem was the <hi type="italic">dwelling-place of God's name,</hi> and therefore the <hi type="italic">sanctuary,</hi> or <hi type="italic">holy place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.7">v. 7</reference>. In this the enemies did wickedly (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.3">v. 3</reference>), for they destroyed it in downright contempt of God and affront to him. (1.) They <hi type="italic">roared in the midst of God's congregations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.4">v. 4</reference>. There where God's faithful people attended on him with a humble reverent silence, or softly speaking, they roared in a riotous revelling manner, being elated with having made themselves masters of that sanctuary of which they had sometimes heard formidable things. (2.) <hi type="italic">They set up their ensigns for signs.</hi> The banners of their army they set up in the temple (Israel's strongest castle, as long as they kept closely to God) as trophies of their victory. There, where the signs of God's presence used to be, now the enemy had set up their ensigns. This daring defiance of God and his power touched his people in a tender part. (3.) They took a pride in destroying <hi type="italic">the carved work</hi> of the temple. As much as formerly men thought it an honour to lend a hand to the building of the temple, and he was thought famous that helped to fell timber for that work, so much now they valued themselves upon their agency in destroying it, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.5-Ps.74.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Thus, as formerly those were celebrated for wise men that did service to religion, so now those are applauded as wits that help to run it down. Some read it thus: <hi type="italic">They show themselves, as one that lifts up axes on high in a thicket of trees,</hi> for so do they break down the carved work of the temple they make no more scruple of breaking down the rich wainscot of the temple than woodcutters do of hewing trees in the forest; such indignation have they at the sanctuary that the most curious carving that ever was seen is beaten down by the common soldiers without any regard had to it, either as a dedicated thing or as a piece of exquisite art. (4.) They set fire to it, and so violated or <hi type="italic">destroyed it to the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.7">v. 7</reference>. The Chaldeans burnt the house of God, that stately costly fabric, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.19">2 Chron. xxxvi. 19</reference>. And the Romans <hi type="italic">left not there one stone upon another</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.2">Matt. xxiv. 2</reference>), rasing it, rasing it, even to the foundations, till Zion, the holy mountain, was, by Titus Vespasian, ploughed as a field. <div eID="gen11820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11821" type="x-p"/> 2. He complains of the desolations of the synagogues, or schools of the prophets, which, before the captivity, were in use, though much more afterwards. There God's word was read and expounded, and his name praised and called upon, without altars or sacrifices. These also they had a spite to (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let us destroy them together;</hi> not only the temple, but all the places of religious worship and the worshippers with them. <hi type="italic">Let us destroy them together;</hi> let them be consumed in the same flame. Pursuant to this impious resolve they <hi type="italic">burnt up all the synagogues of God in the land</hi> and laid them all waste. So great was their rage against religion that the religious houses, because religious, were all levelled with the ground, that God's worshippers might not glorify God, and edify one another, by meeting in solemn assemblies. <div eID="gen11821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11822" type="x-p"/> III. The great aggravation of all these calamities was that they had no prospect at all of relief, nor could they foresee an end of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">v. 9</reference>): "We see our enemy's sign set up in the sanctuary, but <hi type="italic">we see not our signs,</hi> none of the tokens of God's presence, no hopeful indications of approaching deliverance. <hi type="italic">There is no more any prophet</hi> to tell us how long the trouble will last and when things concerning us shall have an end, that the hope of an issue at last may support us under our troubles." In the captivity in Babylon they had prophets, and had been told how long the captivity should continue, but the day was cloudy and dark (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12">Ezek. xxxiv. 12</reference>), and they had not as yet the comfort of these gracious discoveries. God spoke once, yea, twice, good words and comfortable words, but they perceived them not. Observe, They do not complain, "We see not our armies; there are no men of war to command our forces, nor any to go forth with our hosts;" but, "no prophets, none to tell us how long." This puts them upon expostulating with God, as delaying, 1. To assert his honour (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">How long shall the adversary reproach and blaspheme thy name?</hi> In the desolations of the sanctuary our chief concern should be for the glory of God, that it may not be injured by the blasphemies of those who persecute his people for his sake, because they are his; and therefore our enquiry should be, not "How long shall we be troubled?" but "How long shall God be blasphemed?" 2. To exert his power (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Why withdrawest thou thy hand,</hi> and dost not stretch it out, to deliver thy people and destroy thy enemies? <hi type="italic">Pluck it out of thy bosom,</hi> and be not <hi type="italic">as a man astonished, as a mighty man that cannot save,</hi> or will not," <reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">Jer. xiv. 9</reference>. When the power of enemies is most threatening it is comfortable to fly to the power of God.
entries.1872ebaf743f219a72150f62be49667a9a9d1d08: <div eID="gen11822" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Acknowledgments of Divine Power.</title> <div sID="gen11823" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> For God <hi type="italic">is</hi> my King of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces, <hi type="italic">and</hi> gavest him <hi type="italic">to be</hi> meat to the people inhabiting the wilderness. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou didst cleave the fountain and the flood: thou driedst up mighty rivers. <hi type="super">16</hi> The day <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine, the night also <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine: thou hast prepared the light and the sun. <hi type="super">17</hi> Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter. <div eID="gen11823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11824" type="x-p"/> The lamenting church fastens upon something here which she calls to mind, and <hi type="italic">therefore hath she hope</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Lam.3.21">Lam. iii. 21</reference>), with which she encourages herself and silences her own complaints. Two things quiet the minds of those that are here sorrowing for the solemn assembly:— <div eID="gen11824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11825" type="x-p"/> I. That God is the God of Israel, a God in covenant with his people (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">God is my King of old.</hi> This comes in both as a plea in prayer to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.4">Ps. xliv. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">thou art my King, O God!</hi>) and as a prop to their own faith and hope, to encourage themselves to expect deliverance, considering the <hi type="italic">days of old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.77.5">Ps. lxxvii. 5</reference>. The church speaks as a complex body, the same in every age, and therefore calls God, "My King, my King of old," or, "from antiquity;" he of old put himself into that relation to them and appeared and acted for them in that relation. As Israel's King, he wrought salvation in the midst of the nations of the earth; for what he did, in the government of the world, tended towards the salvation of his church. Several things are here mentioned which God had done for his people as their King of old, which encouraged them to commit themselves to him and depend upon him. <div eID="gen11825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11826" type="x-p"/> 1. He had divided the sea before them when they came out of Egypt, not by the strength of Moses or his rod, but by his own strength; and he that could do that could do any thing. <div eID="gen11826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11827" type="x-p"/> 2. He had destroyed Pharaoh and the Egyptians. Pharaoh was the <hi type="italic">leviathan;</hi> the Egyptians were <hi type="italic">the dragons,</hi> fierce and cruel. Observe, (1.) The victory obtained over these enemies. God broke their heads, baffled their politics, as when Israel, the more they were afflicted by them, multiplied the more. God crushed their powers, though complicated, ruined their country by ten plagues, and at last drowned them all in the Red Sea. <hi type="italic">This is Pharaoh and all his multitude,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.18">Ezek. xxxi. 18</reference>. It was the Lord's doing; none besides could do it, and he did it with a strong hand and an outstretched arm. This was typical of Christ's victory over Satan and his kingdom, pursuant to the first promise, that the seed of the woman should break the serpent's head. (2.) The improvement of this victory for the encouragement of the church: <hi type="italic">Thou gavest him to be meat to the people</hi> of Israel, now going to <hi type="italic">inhabit the wilderness.</hi> The spoil of the Egyptians enriched them; they stripped their slain, and so got the Egyptians' arms and weapons, as before they had got their jewels. Or, rather, this providence was meat to their faith and hope, to support and encourage them in reference to the other difficulties they were likely to meet with in the wilderness. It was part of the spiritual meat which they were all made to eat of. Note, The breaking of the heads of the church's enemies is the joy and strength of the hearts of the church's friends. Thus the companions make a banquet even of leviathan, <reference osisRef="Job.41.6">Job xli. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen11827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11828" type="x-p"/> 3. God had both ways altered the course of nature, both in fetching streams out of the rock and turning streams into rock, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.15">v. 15</reference>. (1.) He had dissolved the rock into waters: <hi type="italic">Thou didst bring out the fountain and the flood</hi> (so some read it); and every one knows whence it was brought, out of the rock, out of the flinty rock. Let this never be forgotten, but let it especially be remembered that the rock was Christ, and the waters out of it were spiritual drink. (2.) He had congealed the waters into rock: <hi type="italic">Thou driedst up mighty</hi> rapid <hi type="italic">rivers,</hi> Jordan particularly at the time when it overflowed all its banks. He that did these things could now deliver his oppressed people, and break the yoke of the oppressors, as he had done formerly; nay, he would do it, for his justice and goodness, his wisdom and truth, are still the same, as well as his power. <div eID="gen11828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11829" type="x-p"/> II. That the God of Israel is the God of nature, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.16-Ps.74.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. It is he that orders the regular successions and revolutions, 1. Of day and night. He is the Lord of all time. The evening and the morning are of his ordaining. It is he that opens the eyelids of the morning light, and draws the curtains of the evening shadow. <hi type="italic">He has prepared the moon and the sun</hi> (so some read it), the two great lights, to rule by day and by night alternately. The preparing of them denotes their constant readiness and exact observance of their time, which they never miss a moment. 2. Of summer and winter: "Thou hast <hi type="italic">appointed all the bounds of the earth,</hi> and the different climates of its several regions, for <hi type="italic">thou hast made summer and winter,</hi> the frigid and the torrid zones; or, rather, the constant revolutions of the year and its several seasons." Herein we are to acknowledge God, from whom all the laws and powers of nature are derived; but how does this come in here? (1.) He that had power at first to settle, and still to preserve, this course of nature by the diurnal and annual motions of the heavenly bodies, has certainly all power both to save and to destroy, and with him nothing is impossible, nor are any difficulties or oppositions insuperable. (2.) He that is faithful to his covenant with the day and with the night, and preserves the ordinances of heaven inviolable will certainly make good his promise to his people and never cast off those whom he has chosen, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.36">Jer. xxxi. 35, 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.20-Jer.33.21">xxxiii. 20, 21</reference>. His covenant with Abraham and his seed is as firm as that with Noah and his sons, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Gen. viii. 21</reference>. (3.) Day and night, summer and winter, being counterchanged in the course of nature, throughout all the borders of the earth, we can expect no other than that trouble and peace, prosperity and adversity, should be, in like manner, counterchanged in all the borders of the church. We have as much reason to expect affliction as to expect night and winter. But we have then no more reason to despair of the return of comfort than we have to despair of day and summer.
entries.3d523cf059362010c020a9ab62f03936404229aa: <div eID="gen11829" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Earnest Supplications; Pleading with God.</title> <div sID="gen11830" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Remember this, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the enemy hath reproached, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and <hi type="italic">that</hi> the foolish people have blasphemed thy name. <hi type="super">19</hi> O deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude <hi type="italic">of the wicked:</hi> forget not the congregation of thy poor for ever. 20 Have respect unto the covenant: for the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty. <hi type="super">21</hi> O let not the oppressed return ashamed: let the poor and needy praise thy name. <hi type="super">22</hi> Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily. <hi type="super">23</hi> Forget not the voice of thine enemies: the tumult of those that rise up against thee increaseth continually. <div eID="gen11830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11831" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here, in the name of the church, most earnestly begs that God would appear fro them against their enemies, and put an end to their present troubles. To encourage his own faith, he interests God in this matter (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Arise, O God! plead thy own cause.</hi> This we may be sure he will do, for he is jealous for his own honour; whatever is his own cause he will plead it with a strong hand, will appear against those that oppose it and with and for those that cordially espouse it. He will arise and plead it, though for a time he seems to neglect it; he will stir up himself, will manifest himself, will do his own work in his own time. Note, The cause of religion is God's own cause and he will certainly plead it. Now, to make it out that the cause is God's, he pleads, <div eID="gen11831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11832" type="x-p"/> I. That the persecutors are God's sworn enemies: "Lord, they have not only abused us, but they have been, and are, abusive to thee; what is done against us, for thy sake, does, by consequence, reflect upon thee. But that is not all; they have directly and immediately reproached thee, and <hi type="italic">blasphemed thy name,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.74.18">v. 18</reference>. This was that which they roared in the sanctuary; they triumphed as if they had now got the mastery of the God is Israel, of whom they had heard such great things. As nothing grieves the saints more than to hear God's name blasphemed, so nothing encourages them more to hope that God will appear against their enemies than when they have arrived at such a pitch of wickedness as to reproach God himself; this fills the measure of their sins apace and hastens their ruin. The psalmist insists much upon this: "We dare not answer their reproaches; Lord, do thou answer them. Remember that the <hi type="italic">foolish people have blasphemed thy name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.18">v. 18</reference>) and that still <hi type="italic">the foolish man reproaches thee daily.</hi>" Observe the character of those that reproach God; they are foolish. As atheism is folly (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Ps. xiv. 1</reference>), profaneness and blasphemy are no less so. Perhaps those are cried up as the wits of the age that ridicule religion and sacred things; but really they are the greatest fools, and will shortly be made to appear so before all the world. And yet see their malice—They reproach God daily, as constantly as his faithful worshippers pray to him and praise him; see their impudence—They do not hide their blasphemous thoughts in their own bosoms, but proclaim them with a loud voice (<hi type="italic">forget not the voice of thy enemies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.23">v. 23</reference>), and this with a daring defiance of divine justice; they <hi type="italic">rise up against thee,</hi> and by their blasphemies even wage war with heaven and take up arms against the Almighty. Their noise and <hi type="italic">tumult ascend continually</hi> (so some), as the cry of Sodom came up before God, calling for vengeance, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.21">Gen. xviii. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">It increases continually</hi> (so we read it); they grow worse and worse, and are hardened in their impieties by their successes. Now, Lord, <hi type="italic">remember this; do not forget it.</hi> God needs not to be put in remembrance by us of what he has to do, but thus we must show our concern for his honour and believe that he will vindicate us. <div eID="gen11832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11833" type="x-p"/> II. That the persecuted are his covenant-people. 1. See what distress they are in. They have fallen into the hands of <hi type="italic">the multitude of the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">How are those increased that trouble them!</hi> There is no standing before an enraged multitude, especially like these, armed with power; and, as they are numerous, so they are barbarous: <hi type="italic">The dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty.</hi> The land of the Chaldeans, where there was none of the light of the knowledge of the true God (though otherwise it was famed for learning and arts), was indeed a dark place; the inhabitants of it were <hi type="italic">alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that was in them,</hi> and therefore they were cruel: where there was no true divinity there was scarcely to be found common humanity. They were especially cruel to the people of God; certainly those have no knowledge who <hi type="italic">eat them up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Ps. xiv. 4</reference>. They are oppressed (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.21">v. 21</reference>) because they are poor and unable to help themselves; they are oppressed, and so impoverished and made poor. 2. See what reason they had to hope that God would appear for their relief and not suffer them to be always thus trampled upon. Observe how the psalmist pleads with God for them. (1.) "It is <hi type="italic">thy turtle-dove</hi> that is ready to be swallowed up by the multitude of the wicked," <reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">v. 19</reference>. The church is a dove for harmlessness and mildness, innocency and inoffensiveness, purity and fruitfulness, a dove for mournfulness in a day of distress, a turtle-dove for fidelity and the constancy of love: turtle-doves and pigeons were the only fowls that were offered in sacrifice to God. "Shall thy turtle-dove, that is true to thee and devoted to thy honour, be delivered, its life and soul and all, into the <hi type="italic">hand of the multitude of the wicked,</hi> to whom it will soon become an easy and acceptable prey? Lord, it will be thy honour to help the weak, especially to help thy own." (2.) "It is <hi type="italic">the congregation of thy poor,</hi> and they are not the less thine for their being poor (for God has <hi type="italic">chosen the poor of this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jam. ii. 5</reference>), but they have the more reason to expect thou wilt appear for them because they are many: it is <hi type="italic">the congregation of thy poor;</hi> let them not be abandoned and forgotten for ever." (3.) "They are in covenant with thee; and wilt thou not <hi type="italic">have respect unto the covenant?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.20">v. 20</reference>. Wilt thou not perform the promises thou hast, in thy covenant, made to them? Wilt thou not own those whom thou hast brought into the bond of the covenant?" When God delivers his people it is <hi type="italic">in remembrance of his covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">Lev. xxvi. 42</reference>. "Lord, though we are unworthy to be respected, yet have respect to the covenant." (4.) "They trust in thee, and boast of their relation to thee and expectations from thee. O let not them return ashamed of their hope (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.21">v. 21</reference>), as they will be if they be disappointed." (5.) "If thou deliver them, they will praise thy name and give thee the glory of their deliverance. Appear, Lord, for those that will praise thy name, against those that blaspheme it."  <chapter eID="Ps.74"/> <div eID="gen11833" type="x-p"/>

entries.8edc6a92b0f5640ba2d288c0c5778729b74cb3e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6322"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 74</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.1-Ps.74.23">Psa 74:1-23</reference>. If the historical allusions of <reference osisRef="Ps.74.6-Ps.74.8">Psa 74:6-8</reference>, &c., be referred, as is probable, to the period of the captivity, the author was probably a descendant and namesake of Asaph, David's contemporary and singer (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.15">2Ch 35:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.41">Ezr 2:41</reference>). entries.8958ffdbc7f17e28ae976acb7f2322e2b3e83daf: <div eID="gen20991" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20992" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20993" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20993" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20992" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20994" type="x-p"/> The psalmtst complains of the desolations of the sanctuary, and pleads with God, <reference osisRef="Psa.74.1-Psa.74.3">Psa 74:1-3</reference>; shows the insolence and wickedness of their enemies <reference osisRef="Psa.74.4-Psa.74.8">Psa 74:4-8</reference>; prays to God to act for them as he had done for their fathers, whom, by his miraculous power, he had saved, <reference osisRef="Psa.74.9-Psa.74.17">Psa 74:9-17</reference>; begs God to arise, and vindicate his own honor against his enemies, and the enemies of his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.74.18-Psa.74.23">Psa 74:18-23</reference>. <div eID="gen20994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20995" type="x-p"/> The title is, Maschil of Asaph, or, "A Psalm of Asaph, to give instruction." That this Psalm was written at a time when the temple was ruined, Jerusalem burnt, and the prophets scattered or destroyed, is evident. But it is not so clear whether the desolations here refer to the days of Nebuchadnezzar, or to the desolation that took place under the Romans about the seventieth year of the Christian era. Calmet inclines to the former opinion; and supposes the Psalm to be a lamentation over the temple destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar. <div eID="gen20995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20996" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20997" type="x-p"/> O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? - Hast thou determined that we shall never more be thy people? Are we never to see an end to our calamities?
entries.75409cd47fafcf6b6fa9bef114c9474466168969: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20998" type="x-p"/> Remember thy congregation, which thou hast purchased of old - We are the descendants of that people whom thou didst take unto thyself; the children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Wilt thou never more be reconciled to us?
entries.586ec477a9e53420b3a03153a8a21b43f6ead184: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20999" type="x-p"/> Lift up thy feet - Arise, and return to us, our desolations still continue. Thy sanctuary is profaned by thine and our enemies.
entries.49e448d1f626de4db4f968e8859725c4b7013631: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21000" type="x-p"/> Thine enemies roar - Thy people, who were formerly a distinct and separate people, and who would not even touch a Gentile, are now obliged to mingle with the most profane. Their boisterous mirth, their cruel mockings, their insulting commands, are heard every where in all our assemblies. <div eID="gen21000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21001" type="x-p"/> They set up their ensigns for signs - שמו אותתם אתות samu othotham othoth, they set up their standards in the place of ours. All the ensigns and trophies were those of our enemies; our own were no longer to be seen. <div eID="gen21001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21002" type="x-p"/> The fifth, sixth, and seventh verses give a correct historical account of the ravages committed by the Babylonians, as we may see from <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.4">2Kgs 25:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.7-2Kgs.25.9">2Kgs 25:7-9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.52.7">Jer 52:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.18">Jer 52:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.19">Jer 52:19</reference> : "And the city was broken up, and all the men fled by night by the way of the gate. They took Zedekiah, and slew his sons before his eyes; and put out his eyes, and bound him with fetters of brass, and carried him to Babylon. And on the second day of the fifth month of the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, came unto Jerusalem; and he burnt the house of the Lord, and the king's house, and every great man's house; and all the houses of Jerusalem burnt he with fire. And they broke down the walls of Jerusalem round about. And the pillars of brass and the bases, and the brazen sea, they broke in pieces, and carried the brass to Babylon. And the pots, shovels, snuffers and spoons, and the fire pans and bowls, and such things as were of gold and silver, they took away." Thus they broke down, and carried away, and destroyed this beautiful house; and in the true barbarian spirit, neither sanctity, beauty, symmetry, nor elegance of workmanship, was any thing in their eyes. What hammers and axes could ruin, was ruined; Jerusalem was totally destroyed, and its walls laid level with the ground. Well might the psalmist sigh over such a desolation.
entries.31caf6e8452bd777c4239518c2f23b24de9be01a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21003" type="x-p"/> Let us destroy them - Their object was totally to annihilate the political existence of the Jewish people. <div eID="gen21003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21004" type="x-p"/> They have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land - It is supposed that there were no synagogues in the land till after the Babylonish captivity. How then could the Chaldeans burn up any in Judea? The word מועדי moadey, which we translate synagogues, may be taken in a more general sense, and mean any places where religious assemblies were held: and that such places and assemblies did exist long before the Babylonish captivity, is pretty evident from different parts of Scripture. It appears that Elisha kept such at his house on the sabbaths and new moons. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.23">2Kgs 4:23</reference>. And perhaps to such St. James may refer, <reference osisRef="Act.15.23">Act 15:23</reference>, a species of synagogues, where the law was read of old, in every city of the land. And it appears that such religious meetings were held at the house of the Prophet Ezekiel, <reference osisRef="Eze.33.31">Eze 33:31</reference>. And perhaps every prophet's house was such. This is the only place in the Old Testament where we have the word synagogue. Indeed, wherever there was a place in which God met with patriarch or prophet, and any memorial of it was preserved, there was a מועד moed, or place of religious meeting; and all such places the Chaldeans would destroy, pursuant to their design to extinguish the Jewish religion, and blot out all its memorials from the earth. And this was certainly the most likely means to effect their purpose. How soon would Christianity be destroyed in England if all the churches, chapels, and places of worship were destroyed, and only the poor of the people left in the land; who, from their circumstances, could not build a place for the worship of God! After such desolation, what a miracle was the restoration of the Jews!
entries.3419849328891b9e4214ba320caa7038542cd024: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21005" type="x-p"/> We see not our signs - "They have taken away all our trophies, and have left us no memorial that God has been among us. Even thou thyself hast left us destitute of all those supernatural evidences that have so often convinced us that thou wert among us of a truth." But we may say that they were not totally destitute even of these. The preservation of Daniel in the lion's den, and of the three Hebrews in the fiery furnace; the metamorphosis of Nebuchadnezzar; the handwriting that appeared to Belshazzar; were all so many prodigies and evidences that God had not left them without proofs of his being and his regard. <div eID="gen21005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21006" type="x-p"/> There is no more any prophet - There was not one among them in that place that could tell them how long that captivity was yet to endure. But there were prophets in the captivity. Daniel was one; but his prophecies were confined to one place. Ezekiel was another, but he was among those captives who were by the river Chebar. They had not, as usual, prophets who went to and fro through the land, preaching repentance and remission of sins.
entries.9fbf16d397a768fb67199b3f889e8d3386f0bcb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21007" type="x-p"/> Why withdrawest thou thy hand - It has been remarked, that as the outward habit of the easterns had no sleeves, the hands and arms were frequently covered with the folds of the robe; and in order to do any thing, the hand must be disentangled and drawn out. The literal version of the Hebrew is: "To what time wilt thou draw back thy hand; yea, thy right hand, from within thy bosom?" Consomme; that is, manifest thy power, and destroy thy adversaries. I have, in the introduction to the book of Psalms, spoken of the old metrical version by Sternhold and Hopkins, and have stated that it was formed from the original text. A proof of this may be seen by the learned reader in this and the preceding verse; where, though their version is harsh, and some of their expressions quaint almost to ridicule, yet they have hit the true mean ing which our prose translators have missed: - <reference osisRef="Psa.74.10">Psa 74:10</reference> When wilt thou once, Lord, end this shame,And cease thine en'mies strong?Shall they always blaspheme thy name,And rail on thee so long? <reference osisRef="Psa.74.11">Psa 74:11</reference> Why dost thou draw thy hand aback,And hide it in thy lap?O pluck it out, and be not slackTo give thy foes a rap!
entries.08a37f9cc27ff24bf3f193b3ff8b76a948d97dd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21008" type="x-p"/> For God is my King of old - We have always acknowledged thee as our sovereign; and thou hast reigned as a king in the midst of our land, dispensing salvation and deliverance from the center to every part of the circumference.
entries.80afee8619c71f641f7a58997a906d6d145ffbcb: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21009" type="x-p"/> Thou didst divide the sea - When our fathers came from Egypt. <div eID="gen21009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21010" type="x-p"/> Thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters - Pharaoh, his captains, and all his hosts were drowned in the Red Sea, when attempting to pursue them.
entries.3d0411d4818009097f4bcf3f45e923829c7a4ee5: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21011" type="x-p"/> The heads of leviathan - Leviathan might be intended here as a personification of the Egypttan government; and its heads, Pharaoh and his chief captains. <div eID="gen21011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21012" type="x-p"/> To the people inhabiting the wilderness - Probably meaning the birds and beasts of prey. These were the people of the wilderness, which fed on the dead bodies of the Egyptians, which the tides had cast ashore. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic read, "Thou hast given him for meat to the Ethiopians," or Abyssinians.
entries.303e678c6935ea3b0ebfcfea63e13d687c02ebba: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21013" type="x-p"/> Thou didst cleave the fountain - Thou didst cleave the rock in the wilderness, of which all the congregation drank. <div eID="gen21013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21014" type="x-p"/> Thou driedst up mighty rivers - Does not this refer to the cutting off the waters of the Jordan, so that the people passed over dryshod?
entries.18a2e6123a0415c97e0f1c0881c8e119718d743e: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen21014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21015" type="x-p"/> The day is thine, the night also is thine - Thou art the Author of light, and of the sun, which is the means of dispensing it.
entries.73dc6f6bfbc12ffa9110b7ef7bbabced8dcab4d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen21015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21016" type="x-p"/> Thou hast set all the borders of the earth - Thou alone art the Author of all its grand geographical divisions. <div eID="gen21016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21017" type="x-p"/> Thou hast made summer and winter - Thou hast appointed that peculiarity in the poise and rotation of the earth, by which the seasons are produced.
entries.ee7f8d77b20422b73ffcfa4efc28a0fce37b1341: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen21017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21018" type="x-p"/> Remember this - The heathen not only deny these things, but give the honor of them to their false gods, and thus blaspheme thy name.
entries.6738b55b8f1a03c67d88c66076440c4d3dc0f6df: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen21018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21019" type="x-p"/> Deliver not the soul of thy turtle-dove - Thy people Israel are helpless, defenceless, miserable, and afflicted: O deliver them no longer into the power of their brutal adversaries.
entries.10ec22716c1c99246fb835517e3b0aa4c03478fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen21019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21020" type="x-p"/> Have respect unto the covenant - הבט לברית habbet labberith. Pay attention to the covenant sacrifice; to that offered by Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9">Gen 15:9</reference>, etc., when the contracting parties, God and Abram, passed through between the separated parts of the covenant sacrifice. An indisputable type of Jesus Christ; and of God and man meeting in his sacrificed humanity. <div eID="gen21020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21021" type="x-p"/> The dark places of the earth - The caves, dens, woods, etc., of the land are full of robbers, cut-throats, and murderers, who are continually destroying thy people, so that the holy seed seems as if it would be entirely cut off and the covenant promise thus be rendered void. <div eID="gen21021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21022" type="x-p"/> The words may either apply to Chaldea or Judea. Judea was at this time little else than a den of robbers, its own natural inhabitants being removed. Chaldea was infested with hordes of banditti also.
entries.660aff3873aad87afcf4ab364b33ac87aca1bdc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen21022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21023" type="x-p"/> Let not the oppressed return ashamed - Do not permit thy people to be so diminished, that when, according to thy promise, they are restored to their own land, they may appear to be but a handful of men.
entries.bdcf6e427be92f8654e1d5b9b0bcbb3e75204696: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen21023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21024" type="x-p"/> Plead thine own cause - Thy honor is concerned, as well as our safety and salvation. The fool - the idolater, reproacheth thee daily - he boasts of the superiority of his idols, by whose power, he asserts, we are brought under their domination.
entries.b2430d4ce279a292b04fed4112039658f8abd53b: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen21024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21025" type="x-p"/> Forget not the voice - While we pray to thee for our own salvation, we call upon thee to vindicate thy injured honor: and let all the nations see that thou lovest thy followers, and hatest those who are thy enemies. Let not man prevail against thee or thine.  <chapter eID="Ps.74"/> <div eID="gen21025" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b97afe4f4e3f3b072908ddf61fd5e13ebafd600: <reference osisRef="Ps.74.1-Ps.74.3">Psa 74:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9755" type="x-p"/> The poet begins with the earnest prayer that God would again have compassion upon His church, upon which His judgment of anger has fallen, and would again set up the ruins of Zion. Why for ever (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.10">Psa 74:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.5">Psa 79:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.47">Psa 89:47</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.13.2">Psa 13:2</reference>)? is equivalent to, why so continually and, as it seems, without end? The preterite denotes the act of casting off, the future, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">Psa 74:1</reference></hi>, that lasting condition of this casting off. למה, when the initial of the following word is a guttural, and particularly if it has a merely half-vowel (although in other instances also, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.19">Gen 12:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.27.45">Gen 27:45</reference>; Sol 1:7), is deprived of its <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> and accented on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>, in order (as Mose ha-Nakdan expressly observes) to guard against the swallowing up of the <hi type="italic">ah</hi>; cf. on Psa 10:1. Concerning the smoking of anger, vid., Psa 18:9. The characteristically Asaphic expression צאן מרעיתו is not less Jeremianic, Jer 23:1. In <reference osisRef="Ps.74.2">Psa 74:2</reference> God is reminded of what He has once done for the congregation of His people. קדם, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.2">Psa 44:2</reference>, points back into the Mosaic time of old, to the redemption out of Egypt, which is represented in קנה (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.17">Exo 15:17</reference>) as a purchasing, and in גאל (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.15">Psa 77:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.35">Psa 78:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.13">Exo 15:13</reference>) as a ransoming (<hi type="italic">redemptio</hi>). שׁבט נחלתך is a factitive object; שׁבט is the name given to the whole nation in its distinctness of race from other peoples, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.16">Jer 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.19">Jer 51:19</reference>, cf. Isa 63:17. זה (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.2">Psa 74:2</reference></hi>) is rightly separated from הר־ציון (<hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>); it stands directly for אשׁר, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.8">Psa 104:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.26">Psa 104:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.22">Pro 23:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.17">Job 15:17</reference> (Ges. §122, 2). The congregation of the people and its central abode are, as though forgotten of God, in a condition which sadly contrasts with their election. משּׁאות נצח are ruins (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.73.18">Psa 73:18</reference>) in a state of such total destruction, that all hope of their restoration vanishes before it; נצח here looks forward, just as עולם (חרבות), <reference osisRef="Isa.63.12">Isa 63:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.4">Psa 61:4</reference>, looks backwards. May God then lift His feet up high (פּעמים poetical for רגלים, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.58.11">Psa 58:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.68.24">Psa 68:24</reference>), i.e., with long hurried steps, without stopping, move towards His dwelling - lace that now lies in ruins, that by virtue of His interposition it may rise again. Hath the enemy made merciless havoc - he hath ill-treated (הרע, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Psa 44:3</reference>) everything (כּל, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.8.7">Psa 8:7</reference>, Zep 1:2, for חכּל or את־כּל) in the sanctuary - how is it possible that this sacrilegious vandalism should remain unpunished!
entries.cc188c2fcb2e949ba69aa501877668aa4743025f: <reference osisRef="Ps.74.4-Ps.74.8">Psa 74:4-8</reference> <div eID="gen9755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9756" type="x-p"/> The poet now more minutely describes how the enemy has gone on. Since קדשׁ in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.3">Psa 74:3</reference> is the Temple, מועדיך in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.4">Psa 74:4</reference> ought likewise to mean the Temple with reference to the several courts; but the plural would here (cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.8">Psa 74:8</reference></hi>) be misleading, and is, too, only a various reading. Baer has rightly decided in favour of מועדך;<note placement="foot">The reading מעודיך is received, e.g., by Elias Hutter and Nissel; the Targum translates it, Kimchi follows it in his interpretation, and Abraham of Zante follows it in his paraphrase; it is tolerably widely known, but, according to the lxx and Syriac versions and MSS, it is to be rejected.</note> מועד, as in Lam 2:6., is the instituted (Num 17:1-13 :19 [4]) place of God’s intercourse with His congregation (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">mı̂‛âd</hi>, a rendezvous). What Jeremiah says in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.7">Lam 2:7</reference> (cf. שׁאג, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.15">Jer 2:15</reference>) is here more briefly expressed. By אותתם (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.4">Psa 74:4</reference></hi>) we must not understand military insignia; the scene of the Temple and the supplanting of the Israelitish national insignia to be found there, by the substitution of other insignia, requires that the word should have the religious reference in which it is used of circumcision and of the Sabbath (<reference osisRef="Exod.31.13">Exo 31:13</reference>); such heathen אתות, which were thrust upon the Temple and the congregation of Jahve as henceforth the lawful ones, were those which are set forth in 1 Macc. 1:45-49, and more particularly the so-called abomination of desolation mentioned in v. 54 of the same chapter. With יוּדע (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.5">Psa 74:5</reference>) the terrible scene which was at that time taking place before their eyes (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.10">Psa 79:10</reference>) is introduced. כּמביא is the subject; it became visible, tangible, noticeable, i.e., it looked, and one experienced it, as if a man caused the axe to enter into the thicket of the wood, i.e., struck into or at it right and left. The plural קדּמּות forces itself into the simile because it is the many heathen warriors who are, as in Jer 46:22., likened to these hewers of wood. Norzi calls the <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> of בסבך־עץ <hi type="italic">Kametz chatuph</hi>; the combining form would then be a contraction of סבך (Ewald, Olshausen), for the long <hi type="italic">ā</hi> of סבך does not admit of any contraction. According to another view it is to be read <hi type="italic">bi - sbāch - etz</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Esth.4.8">Est 4:8</reference> <hi type="italic">kethāb - hadāth</hi> with counter-tone <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> beside the long vowel, as e.g., עץ־הגּן, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.16">Gen 2:16</reference>). The poet follows the work of destruction up to the destroying stroke, which is introduced by the ועת (perhaps ועת, <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> ועתּה), which arrests one’s attention. In <reference osisRef="Ps.74.5">Psa 74:5</reference> the usual, unbroken quiet is depicted, as is the heavy Cyclopean labour in the Virgilian <hi type="italic">illi inter sese</hi>, etc.; in <hi type="italic">jahalomûn</hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.6">Psa 74:6</reference></hi> (now and then pointed <hi type="italic">jahlomûn</hi>), we hear the stroke of the uplifted axes, which break in pieces the costly carved work of the Temple. The suffix of פּתּוּחיה (the carved works thereof) refers, according to the sense, to מועדך. The lxx, favouring the Maccabaean interpretation, renders: ἐξέκοψαν τάς θύρας αὐτῆς (פּתחיה). This shattering of the panelling is followed in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.7">Psa 74:7</reference> by the burning, first of all, as we may suppose, of this panelling itself so far as it consists of wood. The guaranteed reading here is מקדשׁך, not מקדשׁיך. שׁלּח בּאשׁ signifies to set on fire, <hi type="italic">immittere igni</hi>, differing from שׁלּח אשׁ בּ, to set fire to, <hi type="italic">immittere ignem</hi>. On לארץ חלּלוּ, cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.2.2">Lam 2:2</reference>; Jer 19:13. Hitzig, following the lxx, Targum, and Jerome, derives the exclamation of the enemies נינם from נין: their whole generation (viz., we will root out)! But נין is posterity, descendants; why therefore only the young and not the aged? And why is it an expression of the object and not rather of the action, the object of which would be self-evident? נינם is <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> of ינה, here = <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הונה, to force, oppress, tyrannize over, and like אנס, to compel by violence, in later Hebrew. נינם (from יינה, like ייפה) is changed in pause into נינם; cf. the future forms in Num 21:30; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.19">Exo 34:19</reference>, and also in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.10">Psa 118:10</reference>-12. Now, after mention has been made of the burning of the Temple framework, מועדי־אל cannot denote the place of the divine manifestation after its divisions (Hengstenberg), still less the festive assemblies (Böttcher), which the enemy could only have burnt up by setting fire to the Temple over their heads, and כל does not at all suit this. The expression apparently has reference to synagogues (and this ought not to be disputed), as Aquila and Symmachus render the word. For there is no room for thinking of the separate services conducted by the prophets in the northern kingdom (2Ki 4:23), because this kingdom no longer existed at the time this Psalm was written; nor of the בּמות, the burning down of which no pious Israelite would have bewailed; nor of the sacred places memorable from the early history of Israel, which are nowhere called מועדים, and after the founding of the central sanctuary appear only as the seats of false religious rites. The expression points (like בּית ועד, <hi type="italic">Sota</hi> ix. 15) to places of assembly for religious purposes, to houses for prayer and teaching, that is to say, to synagogues - a weighty instance in favour of the Maccabaean origin of the Psalm.
entries.9fa324b5cd6ccdd9c1f27432aff61bd3a25861b5: <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9-Ps.74.11">Psa 74:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen9756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9757" type="x-p"/> The worst thing the poet has to complain of is that God has not acknowledged His people during this time of suffering as at other times. “Our signs” is the direct antithesis to “their sings” (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.4">Psa 74:4</reference>), hence they are not to be understood, after <reference osisRef="Ps.86.17">Psa 86:17</reference>, as signs which God works. The suffix demands, besides, something of a perpetual character; they are the instituted ordinances of divine worship by means of which God is pleased to stand in fellowship with His people, and which are now no longer to be seen because the enemies have set them aside. The complaint “there is not prophet any more” would seem strange in the period immediately after the destruction of Jerusalem, for Jeremiah’s term of active service lasted beyond this. Moreover, a year before (in the tenth year of Zedekiah’s reign) he had predicted that the Babylonian domination, and relatively the Exile, would last seventy years; besides, six years before the destruction Ezekiel appeared, who was in communication with those who remained behind in the land. The reference to <reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">Lam 2:9</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.26">Eze 7:26</reference>) does not satisfy one; for there it is assumed that there were prophets, a fact which is here denied. Only perhaps as a voice coming out of the Exile, the middle of which (cf. Hos 3:4; <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2Ch 15:3</reference>, and besides <hi type="italic">Canticum trium puerorum</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Psa 74:14</reference> : καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τούτῳ ἄρχων καὶ προφήτης καὶ ἡγούμενος) was truly thus devoid of signs or miracles, and devoid of the prophetic word of consolation, can <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Psa 74:9</reference> be comprehended. The seventy years of Jeremiah were then still a riddle without any generally known solution (Dan. 9). If, however, synagogues are meant in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.8">Psa 74:8</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Psa 74:9</reference> now too accords with the like-sounding lament in the calamitous times of Antiochus (1 Macc. 4:46; 9:27; 14:41). In <reference osisRef="Ps.74.10">Psa 74:10</reference> the poet turns to God Himself with the question “How long?” how long is this (apparently) endless blaspheming of the enemy to last? Why dost Thou draw back (viz., ממּנוּ, from us, not עלינוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.81.15">Psa 81:15</reference>) Thy hand and Thy right hand? The conjunction of synonyms “Thy hand and Thy right hand” is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.4">Psa 44:4</reference>, Sirach 33:7, a fuller expression for God’s omnipotent energy. This is now at rest; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.11">Psa 74:11</reference></hi> calls upon it to give help by an act of judgment. “Out of the midst of Thy bosom, destroy,” is a pregnant expression for, “drawing forth out of Thy bosom the hand that rests inactive there, do Thou destroy.” The <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> חוקך has perhaps the same meaning; for חוק, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥawq</hi>, signifies, like חיק, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥayq</hi>, the act of encompassing, then that which encompasses. Instead of מחיקך (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.7">Exo 4:7</reference>) the expression is מקּרב חיקך, because there, within the realm of the bosom, the punitive justice of God for a time as it were slumbers. On the כלּה, which outwardly is without any object, cf. Psa 59:14.
entries.b6bb2b8388298d524f5b2fa875d93260e1df422e: <reference osisRef="Ps.74.12-Ps.74.17">Psa 74:12-17</reference> <div eID="gen9757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9758" type="x-p"/> With this prayer for the destruction of the enemies by God’s interposition closes the first half of the Psalm, which has for its subject-matter the crying contradiction between the present state of things and God’s relationship to Israel. The poet now draws comfort by looking back into the time when God as Israel’s King unfolded the rich fulness of His salvation everywhere upon the earth, where Israel’s existence was imperilled. בּקרב הארץ, not only within the circumference of the Holy Land, but, e.g., also within that of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.18-Exod.8.22">Exo 8:18-22</reference>). The poet has Egypt directly in his mind, for there now follows first of all a glance at the historical (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.13-Ps.74.15">Psa 74:13-15</reference>), and then at the natural displays of God’s power (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.16">Psa 74:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.17">Psa 74:17</reference>). Hengstenberg is of opinion that <reference osisRef="Ps.74.13-Ps.74.15">Psa 74:13-15</reference> also are to be understood in the latter sense, and appeals to <reference osisRef="Job.26.11">Job 26:11</reference>-13. But just as Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>) transfers these emblems of the omnipotence of God in the natural world to His proofs of power in connection with the history of redemption which were exhibited in the case of a worldly power, so does the poet here also in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.13">Psa 74:13</reference>-15. The תּנּיּן (the extended saurian) is in Isaiah, as in Ezekiel (התּנּים, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Psa 29:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.2">Psa 32:2</reference>), an emblem of Pharaoh and of his kingdom; in like manner here the <hi type="italic">leviathan</hi> is the proper natural wonder of Egypt. As a water-snake or a crocodile, when it comes up with its head above the water, is killed by a powerful stroke, did God break the heads of the Egyptians, so that the sea cast up their dead bodies (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.30">Exo 14:30</reference>). The ציּים, the dwellers in the steppe, to whom these became food, are not the Aethiopians (lxx, Jerome), or rather the Ichthyophagi (Bocahrt, Hengstenberg), who according to Agatharcides fed ἐκ τῶν ἐκριπτομένων εἰς τὴν χέρσον κητῶν, but were no cannibals, but the wild beasts of the desert, which are called עם, as in Pro 30:25. the ants and the rock-badgers. לציים is a permutative of the notion לעם, which was not completed: to a (singular) people, viz., to the wild animals of the steppe. <reference osisRef="Ps.74.15">Psa 74:15</reference> also still refers not to miracles of creation, but to miracles wrought in the course of the history of redemption; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.15">Psa 74:15</reference></hi> refers to the giving of water out of the rock (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.15">Psa 78:15</reference>), and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.15">Psa 74:15</reference></hi> to the passage through the Jordan, which was miraculously dried up (הובשׁתּ, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.2.10">Jos 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.4.23">Jos 4:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.5.1">Jos 5:1</reference>). The object מעין ונחל is intended as referring to the result: so that the water flowed out of the cleft after the manner of a fountain and a brook. נהרות are the several streams of the one Jordan; the attributive genitive איתן describe them as streams having an abundance that does not dry up, streams of perennial fulness. The God of Israel who has thus marvellously made Himself known in history is, however, the Creator and Lord of all created things. Day and night and the stars alike are His creatures. In close connection with the night, which is mentioned second, the moon, the מאור of the night, precedes the sun; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.8.4">Psa 8:4</reference>, where כּונן is the same as הכין in this passage. It is an error to render thus: bodies of light, and more particularly the sun; which would have made one expect מאורות before the specializing <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>. גּבוּלות are not merely the bounds of the land towards the sea, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer 5:22</reference>, but, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.32.8">Deu 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Act 17:26</reference>, even the boundaries of the land in themselves, that is to say, the natural boundaries of the inland country. קיץ וחרף are the two halves of the year: summer including spring (אביב), which begins in Nisan, the spring-month, about the time of the vernal equinox, and autumn including winter (צתו), after the termination of which the strictly spring vegetation begins (Sol 2:11). The seasons are personified, and are called God’s formations or works, as it were the angels of summer and of winter.
entries.20827ae6e63dc82e25c4237f80f9947e38bbfac9: <reference osisRef="Ps.74.18-Ps.74.23">Psa 74:18-23</reference> <div eID="gen9758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9759" type="x-p"/> The poet, after he has thus consoled himself by the contemplation of the power of God which He has displayed for His people’s good as their Redeemer, and for the good of the whole of mankind as the Creator, rises anew to prayer, but all the more cheerfully and boldly. Since ever present facts of creation have been referred to just now, and the historical mighty deeds of God only further back, זאת refers rather forwards to the blaspheming of the enemies which He suffers now to go on unpunished, as though He took no cognizance of it. חרף has <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> after it in order to separate the word, which signifies reviling, from the most holy Name. The epithet עם־נבל reminds one of Deu 32:21. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Psa 74:19</reference></hi> according to the accents חיּת is the absolute state (the primary form of חיּה, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1">Psa 61:1</reference>): give not over, abandon not to the wild beast (beasts), the soul of Thy turtle-dove. This is probably correct, since לחיּת נפשׁ, “to the eager wild beast,” this inversion of the well-known expression נפשׁ חיּה, which on the contrary yields the sense of <hi type="italic">vita animae</hi>, is an improbable and exampleless expression. If נפשׁ were intended to be thus understood, the poet might have written אל־תתן לנפשׁ חיּה תורך, “give not Thy turtle-dove over to the desire of the wild beast.” Hupfeld thinks that the “old, stupid reading” may be set right at one stroke, inasmuch as he reads אל תתן לנפש חית תורך, and renders it “give not to rage the life Thy turtle-dove;” but where is any support to be found for this לנפשׁ, “to rage,” or rather (<hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, S. 202; tr. p. 239) “to eager desire?” The word cannot signify this in such an isolated position. Israel, which is also compared to a dove in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.14">Psa 68:14</reference>, is called a turtle-dove (תּור). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Psa 74:19</reference></hi> חיּת has the same signification as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Psa 74:19</reference></hi>, and the same sense as <reference osisRef="Ps.68.11">Psa 68:11</reference> (cf. Ps 69:37): the creatures of Thy miserable ones, i.e., Thy poor, miserable creatures - a figurative designation of the <hi type="italic">ecclesia pressa</hi>. The church, which it is the custom of the Asaphic Psalms to designate with emblematical names taken from the animal world, finds itself now like sheep among wolves, and seems to itself as if it were forgotten by God. The cry of prayer הבּט לבּרית comes forth out of circumstances such as were those of the Maccabaean age. בּרית is the covenant of circumcision (Gen. 17); ); the persecution of the age of the Seleucidae put faith to the severe test, that circumcision, this sign which was the pledge to Israel of God’s gracious protection, became just the sign by which the Syrians knew their victims. In the Book of Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.28">Dan 11:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">Dan 11:30</reference>, cf. Ps. 22:32, ברית is used directly of the religion of Israel and its band of confessors. The confirmatory clause <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.74.20">Psa 74:20</reference> </hi>also corresponds to the Maccabaean age, when the persecuted confessors hid themselves far away in the mountains (1 Macc. 2:26ff., 2 Macc. 6:11), but were tracked by the enemy and slain, - at that time the hiding-places (κρύφοι, 1 Macc. 1:53) of the land were in reality full of the habitations of violence. The combination נאות חמס is like נאות השׁלום, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.37">Jer 25:37</reference>, cf. Gen 6:11. From this point the Psalm draws to a close in more familiar Psalm - strains. אל־ישׁב, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.21">Psa 74:21</reference>, viz., from drawing near to Thee with their supplications. “The reproach of the foolish all the day” is that which incessantly goes forth from them. עלה תּמיד, “going up (<reference osisRef="1Sam.5.12">1Sa 5:12</reference>, not: increasing, 1Ki 22:35) perpetually,” although without the article, is not a predicate, but attributive (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">Psa 57:3</reference>). The tone of the prayer is throughout temperate; this the ground upon which it bases itself is therefore all the more forcible.  <chapter eID="Ps.74"/> <div eID="gen9759" type="x-p"/>
